content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper focuses on motion modelling aspects of the multiple object tracking (MOT) problem. In particular, the authors study limitations of linear motion models and Kalman filter based inference by studying the behavior of the implementation in Simple Online and Realtime Tracking (SORT). They propose the following improvements:

* Reduction of state uncertainty after occlusion by running Kalman filter update steps on virtual measurements. These measurements are generated on a line between the last detection before the occlusion and the first detection after the occlusion.
* An additional cost term for the association metric which takes into account how well detections align the with the orientation of the tracks motion. This term is computed from outside the Kalman filter state (difference between two fixed point positions instead of velocity in state estimate).

Using these modifications, the authors achieve competitive performance on different MOT benchmarks (MOTChallenge, KITTI, DanceTrack).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
* I found the analysis of the behavior of the Kalman filter behind SORT interesting to read. The equations that are used to illustrate issues  are helpful to understand the issues which the paper addresses.
* Based on the provided evaluation, the proposed - in implementation quite simple - adaptations provide competitive performance on benchmarks compared to other, more complex algorithms.

Weaknesses:
* I would enjoy if the proposed changes to the motion modelling would be better embedded in a theoretical framework. For example, the fixed two-point direction computation for the modified association cost is pragmatic, but could we achieve the same or better performance regarding direction compatibility by moving away from the Kalman filter to, for example, a fixed lag smoother? The same holds for the proposed OOS. How is the generation of virtual measurements for Kalman filter update steps justified in the probabilistic framework?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
* The paper is comprehensive in the mathematical analysis of the Kalman filter behavior. Yet, I find some of the conclusions from the derivations surprisingly obvious. For example, "estimating speed between consecutive frames maximizes the noise" (p. 4) and "the scale of noise estimation is negatively correlated to the time difference between two observations" (p. 6). I would consider to remove some of the more complicated equations that lead to simple statements in order to improve readability.
* It is not easy to grasp the essence behind some of the equations. For example, equation 6 shows the sum of two association cost terms, but the concrete design of these is only given in text. The benefit for the reader to have equation 6 in the paper is marginal without having the design of the consistency cost term C_v.
* To improve clarity, figures should describe how the proposed method works, instead of only illustrating the output for a specific scene.

Novelty:
My main take-a-way from this paper is that linear motion models in a Kalman filter framework do not work well in visual MOT. If we move away from the Kalman filter, because it doesn't work well in the visual MOT setup, research directions that focus on more visual aspects of motion modeling might be more fruitful than fixes around it (e.g. optical flow, learning based methods).

Evaluation:
* Evaluation is performed on different public benchmarks with fixed evaluation protocol and held-out test sets.
* Authors use nonstandard detections, but the detection set is shared with other methods in the benchmark which use the same set.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes pragmatic improvements to an established multiple object tracking algorithm with good results. The improvements are only incremental and they are not well embedded in the theoretical framework of the method which they improve upon. Therefore, I do not see any particular errors, but only marginal significance. The clarity of the writing and graphics can be improved.

content.title: Response to Reviewer ZUmy
content.comment:
We appreciate the suggestions and comments from Reviewer ZUmy. We make responses to the specific questions here. 

**Q1. Could we achieve the same or better performance regarding direction compatibility by moving away from the Kalman filter to, for example, a fixed lag smoother**

**A1.** Choosing a two-point interpolation-based trajectory generation is not just for its being pragmatic but also to align with the linear motion assumption by KF. But you are correct, there can be other hypotheses. And we discussed some common ones in Table 6. 

However, there are three fundamental conflicts preventing us from using smoothers, such as fix-lag and fix-interval smoother to replace the current basic framework:

   1. We are studying online object tracking. Therefore, we could use only past states to determine the state estimations on the current time step. However, the typical smoother would require using states on future time steps to better fit the trajectory on the current step. For example, fix-lag smoother requires the states on time steps $k-N$ -> $k$ to adjust the state on the ($k-N$)-th time step, where $N$ is called the “fixed lag”. So, to apply fix-lag smoother, we have to know the states on future $N$ steps. This breaks the basic requirement in online multi-object tracking because we can't reverse the time in the real world to go back to correct previous results.

   2. Smoothers are usually effective to "optimize" the value of existing data points. However, the problem we face in tracking under occlusion is to correct the biased KF parameters with errors accumulated during no observations where no data points are presented at the period. In such a period, we only have the data points at the first step ("last-seen" step) and the last step ("re-activation" step). Only two data points can't support any commonly used smoothers without pre-defined motion patterns, such as linear motion assumption.

   3. Even if we allow offline postprocessing of tracks, the common practice is only allowing using interpolation to fill missing data points. Adjusting the value of existing footage in a track, which is what smoothers do, is not a common practice in the video multi-object tracking community. For interpolating missing steps on tracks, we make some discussion about the choice of offline interpolation of trajectory in the appendix (Table 9) but that is only secondary and out of the main focus and makes OC-SORT not "Simple, Online, Realtime" anymore.

**Q2. The design of the consistency term C_v needs more clarification.**

**A2.** Yes, we agree that though we discussed in detail about the design of OCM in Appendix A, more details are better presented in the main text. Basically, in our default implementation, $C_v$ is the difference of trajectory directions in radians. We have revised the draft to add more details regarding $C_v$ in Section 4.2. 

**Q3.  Figure 3 can be re-designed to improve clarity.**

**A3.** Thanks for the suggestion. We would consider a better way to illustrate the proposed method more comprehensively and clearly. We are considering possible improvements over Figure 2 to better illustrate the proposed method and mention the behavior difference between OC-SORT and SORT can be better understood by referring to the case study in Figure 6 and Figure 7 in the appendix.

content.title: Response to Reviewer jioH
content.comment:
We appreciate the suggestions and comments from Reviewer jioH. In our original paper, we alread provided the discussion for large-motion cases and with different detecors. Here, we make more detailed response.

**Q1: OC-SORT is less effective to handle large motion cases.**

**A1:** We noticed this limitation and honestly discussed it in Section 5.4. But this limitation does not come from OC-SORT itself but from the commonly used IoU matching. We aim to provide a generalizable implementation and mainly focus on fixing the internal flaws of KF in tracking. So we inherit the common practice of using IoU as the term to associate objects across frames, which is sensitive to large motion and low frame rate. 

By adding other association terms such as C-IoU and center distance, this limitation can be easily fixed. For example, using C-IoU and center distance instead of only IoU in association, OC-SORT achieves HOTA=78.42 for the "Car" category with little harm to time efficiency (FPS=745). When matching the rigid-body objects such as cars, incorporating with appearance matching can further more effective, but that is out of the scope of this work and can't make contributions of OC-SORT.

We hesitated about whether we should adopt different data-specific techniques on different datasets. We finally chose to provide a clean, uniform, and generalizable implementation and report performance based on it. It will more clearly suggest the real contribution of the proposed method without gains from careful tuning parameters and data-specific heuristic tricks. But still, OC-SORT is flexible to incorporate with all the mentioned customizations and we provide the API in the submitted source code as well. In our submitted source code, we provided the implementation to use IoU, C-IoU, D-IoU, G-IoU, center distance etc as the association cost term. Please refer to *trackers/ocsort_tracker/association.py* for details. Also, the DeepSORT implementation we provided can make OC-SORT incorporate with appearance matching as well, which can probably further boost the performance for rigid-body object tracking, such as cars.

**Q2. It is more complete to provide results with more detectors.** 

**A2:** As the detection is not the core of this paper, we only provide the results based on the YOLOX for the private tracking in Table 1 and Table 2. But we agree that OC-SORT can be more convincing if its performance is demonstrated by using other detectors. Therefore, 

1. in Table 4, for the experiments on KITTI, we adopt the detections of PermaTrack instead of YOLOX. The results also suggest the good performance of OC-SORT.

2. in Table 12 and Table 13, we benchmark OC-SORT in the public tracking settings where all methods use the same detector (Faster-RCNN). 

3. in Table 10, we simply adopt the detection results of the other two methods (FairMOT and HeadTrack) and compare the tracking performance with them on the CroHD dataset. The results also suggest the consistent performance gain from OC-SORT.

We provide the source code to reproduce all results in the supplementary results including running OC-SORT with any given detectors. We are confident that OC-SORT can show consistent performance gains given different detectors.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper investigates several limitations in the SORT method for multiple object tracking and proposed an improved version named as Observation-Centric SORT (OC-SORT).  Compared to the vanilla SORT method, the improvements are two-fold: First, when the detector fails to detect an object for a while (usually the object being occluded), the Kalman filter cannot update its states since no observations are given, leading to inaccurate state estimation and thus confuses motion-based association. In OC-SORT, they use appearance cues to associate between observations and lost tracks, and when a lost track is re-activated, the Kalman states in its "being lost" time steps are linearly interpolated to make sure the motion prediction more consistent with the observation.  The second improvement is a new affinity term for association. Previous motion cues used for association considers only the observation state (position), and in OC-SORT, they introduce affinity based on the first-order derivative of the observation state (velocity). This is based on the constant velocity hypothesis of their motion model. Extensive experiments results are given to show the effectiveness of OC-SORT. Results look good especially on a newly-proposed dataset, DanceTrack.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
+ This paper is very-well written. The limitations of previous works are properly discussed, making it  quite easy to understand the motivations. I also like the analysis in the magnitudes of noise (Eq.3, Eq.7). 
+ It is very nice to see a paper discussing the leverage of motion cues in multi-object tracking when almost all the others are more focusing on appearance cues. 
+ The proposed method is quite simple and the implementation details are sufficiently described. It is possible to re-produce it with minimum efforts. 
+ The improvements on a challenging dataset, DanceTrack, looks pretty good, refreshing previous state-of-the-art by 7.3\% in terms of the HOTA metric.

Weakness:
- Despite well-motivated, the proposed method looks incremental and far from elegant. Consider the two technical contributions:
1. The first is adding interpolation to the Kalman states for re-activated tracklets, to let the estimated state pays more attention to the observation (object detection). The implementation is a simple linear interpolation between the last-seen state and the re-activated state. I am curious to know if it is necessary to perform such an interpolation, because it is possible to derive a close-form solution to the re-activated state, without interpolation. 
2. The second contribution is a velocity affinity term for association. Apparently the assumption behind is that the velocity should be constant when the frame rate is high enough ($\Delta t -> 0$), and they wanted to use the velocity cues to help when position cues are inaccurate. The constant volocity assumption is already considered in the vanilla Kalman formulation, so the only difference here is that the velocity is estimated using more history states, and this point itself, is actually a  double-edged sword that requires trade-offs (Appendix A). IMO this additional veolocity affinity would not improve the cases when the vanilla Kalman Filter fails, usually non-linear motions; and on the other hand, if carefully tuning hyper-parameters in the vanilla Kalman Filter, it probably would achieve similar performance compared to using the velocity affinity term. As a baseline, it is necessary to explore how good  the vanilla Kalman Filter can do, because it can be also tuned to be "object-centric'.

- Regarding the experiments: Although results on DanceTrack looks quite nice, performance gain on MOT-17 and MOT-20 seems quite limited, where the motion parttens are relatively simpler. The MOTA metric even degenerates on the two datasets. It is questionable from the results that if the proposed method can be applied to general senerios, or it can only improve specific cases like non-linear moitons in  DanceTrack.

content.title: Response to Reviewer w8YY [2/2]
content.comment:
**Q5: The gain of OC-SORT on MOT17/MOT20 is limited regarding MOTA.**

**A5:** 
* First, MOTA is not a good metric to evaluate tracking performance as it is mainly influenced by the detection recalls instead of association quality. OC-SORT shows lower MOTA than ByteTrack on MOT17/MOT20 because 
   1. OC-SORT recalls fewer detections while ByteTrack takes more detections of low confidence into the final results. A simple experiment is to lower the detection confidence of OC-SORT to be the same as ByteTrack, OC-SORT achieves a comparable MOTA score with ByteTrack on MOT17/MOT20. 
   2. As discussed in Section 5.2,  ByteTrack has a well-tuned threshold setting that sets the detection threshold different on different video sequences in the test set on MOT17/MOT20. If we adopt the same trick, OC-SORT achieves even further higher MOTA. Without the adaptive thresholds, ByteTrack's MOTA will decrease to the same level as OC-SORT. But we think this is not a generalizable practice so we always report the results from shared parameters (of course, fixed detection threshold) on all datasets. We include the implementation of ByteTrack in our submitted code as well, all the claims can be validated. 

* But also, it is correct that OC-SORT shows more advantage than the vanilla SORT when the object motion is non-linear and there is heavy occlusion. But it won't suffer from additional failure when the motion is relatively simpler, such as on MOT17/MOT20, because in such cases, all applied techniques in OCM and OOS degrade to agree with the naive assumption of linear motion, which is shared by vanilla KF-based tracking, such as SORT.
In the appendix, we provide more results with different detectors on MOT17/MOT20 (Table 11, 12, 13) and CroHD (Table 10). All the results demonstrate that the advantage of OC-SORT is consistent. Again, we note that the parameters of OC-SORT are consistent on all datasets, we did no specific parameter tuning to achieve superior performance. 

**Q6: the technical novelty of OC-SORT is limited**

**A6:** We have reviewed the novelty of OC-SORT in the general feedback and the discussion about why OC-SORT can not be imitated by vanilla SORT by tuning the parameters. We believe OC-SORT shows good novelty as it introduces an effective and efficient solution by fixing intrinsic and long-standing flaws of the widely used Kalman Filter in this area. It achieves SoTA performance while keeping online and fast.

**Q7: insufficient exploration and comparison to vanilla Kalman Filter baseline, several hyper-parameters of which can be tuned to make it more “object-centric”**

**A7**: The vanilla Kalman Filter baseline is SORT, whose performance is investigated on DanceTrack in Table 3. Using the detections and the same value for shared parameters. On MOT17 we have 
|         | HOTA | MOTA | IDF1 |
|---------|------|------|------|
| SORT    | 59.8 | 75.4 | 73.3 |
| OC-SORT | 63.2 | 78.0 | 77.5 |

And on MOT20 we have 

|         | HOTA | MOTA | IDF1 |
|---------|------|------|------|
| SORT    | 58.1 | 72.8 | 72.2 |
| OC-SORT | 62.1 | 75.5 | 75.9 |

A similar comparison to the performance of SORT is also available in the paper of ByteTrack[2] and we have provided the code for vanilla SORT in our submitted source code as well. 

**Q8: there are tons of research on improving the vanilla KF that considers the similar "object-centric" topic, several of which are disscussed in the related work section but none compared in the experiment section.**

**A8:** We don't provide another example of "observation-centric" variants of the vanilla KF in the related works. In the first section of "Motion Models", we discuss two lines of related works:
1. some follow-ups and variants of KF, such as Extended KF and Unscented KF. But they are not "observation-centric" at all as they still use the filter estimations as the pivot to predict and update the states. Their contribution is to extend KF to handle non-linear motion situations. However, they rely on pre-defined assumptions of motion patterns, which can not be applied in practice as the non-linear motion in real-time is diverse. This is why these follow-ups of KF are paid little attention to in the area of multi-object tracking. 
2. Some techniques to adjust the data fitting in Bayesian estimation, such as fixed-lag smoother and fixed-interval smoother. However, they are smoothers so they have to use the data points on future time steps. It means that they can't be used for online object tracking. As a secondary part, in the appendix, we discuss some choices of offline trajectory interpolation in Table 9. We even use more advanced Gaussian Process Regression. But they are still interpolation to fill missing data points instead of smoothing to adjust the value of existing data points. Also, all these make the algorithm not online anymore and thus out of the main focus of this paper.

Reference:

[2] “ByteTrack: Multi-Object Tracking by Associating Every Detection Box”

content.title: Response to Reviewer w8YY [1/2]
content.comment:
We appreciate the suggestions and comments from Reviewer w8YY. We would like to clarify some misunderstandings in the review and respond to the specific questions.

**[Misunderstanding] Q1: “In OC-SORT, they use appearance cues to associate between observations and lost tracks”.**

**A1**: In OC-SORT, no appearance features are used during the tracking stage. As we discussed in the abstract, introduction, and following technical sections, we focus on developing a motion-based tracking algorithm in OC-SORT. Given the detections, all the information OC-SORT requires for tracking is only the position of object bounding boxes. 

**[Misunderstanding] Q2: The vanilla Kalman Filter can be turned to be “observation-centric”.**

**A2:**  The concern about the novelty of OC-SORT is partially from the misunderstanding that the vanilla Kalman Filter can also be “observation-centric” by turning its parameters. However, this is not true. We use the term “observation-centric” to emphasize the characteristics of OC-SORT because **(1)** it can use the observations (also called “measurements”, which are the detections from an off-shelf detector) to correct the bias in the filter parameters accumulated during the period of no measurement; **(2)** the motion pattern assumption is not reflected in the predict-update cycles of filter estimations but also directly linked to the observations, which enjoys no temporal error magnification. 

The first point is realized by the design of Observation-Centric Online Smoothing (OOS) and the second is by the use of Observation-Centric Momentum (OCM). 

OOS is designed at the filter level and can’t be supported by the vanilla Kalman Filter with only has the vanilla update and predict stages. To be precise, Kalman Filter has no mechanism to backcheck its parameters on previous time steps to optimize the estimations on the current and future steps. OOS is triggered only when a track is reactivated from being lost and out of the update-predict loop of vanilla Kalman filter.

OCM is designed at the tracker level, namely how to use Kalman Filter to associate detections across frames. The baseline method to use vanilla Kalman Filter for tracking is the classic SORT[1] tracker. However, SORT can’t support OCM by simply tuning parameters as well. The intrinsic conflict is that SORT uses the estimations instead of the observations as the final track footage and the update of estimations (object positions and the first-order derivative) can only reply on the vanilla Kalman Filter, where observation plays no role to reflect the linear motion assumption. However, that is what we exactly need to realize OCM because its core is to use observations instead of estimations to reflect the linear motion assumption in the association.


**Q3: Is the interpolation used to the generated virtual trajectory in OOS necessary? Is it possible to derive a closed-form solution to the re-activated state?**

**A3:** OOS is designed to correct the filter parameters on the steps between the “last-seen” step and the “reactivation” step. The generation of the virtual trajectory (by interpolation) won’t change the state on the reactivation step because that serves as an anchor in the interpolation. We can't confidently understand your meaning of a "closed-form" solution. If you mean we can use the linear motion assumption and Kalman Filter to derive a state on the re-activation step, that is true. But that is actually the core argument of this paper that this state is usually very biased from the true object position because no observation is available on the steps in between to supervise the update of filter parameters (see discussions in Section 3.2.1 and 3.2.2). That is why we need the virtual trajectory to optimize the error accumulated during this period. 

**Q4: The contribution of velocity affinity term for association can be covered by vanilla Kalman Filter.**

**A4:** In the vanilla Kalman filter and its implementation in multi-object tracking, i.e. SORT, the velocity is only used to predict the state on the next time step (Equation 2). The meaning of OCM is not just “using more history states”. The core of OCM is to use observation instead of estimations to follow the assumption of linear motion because the estimations suffer from the sensitivity to state noise (Section 3.2.1) and temporal error magnification (Section 3.2.2). We can’t see a way to tune SORT to make it “observation-centric” without introducing modules like OOS and OCM as OC-SORT does. We provide the implementation of vanilla SORT in our source code in the supplementary material as well. And we compare the performance between OC-SORT and SORT in Table 3, which shows a huge performance gap.

Reference:

[1] "Simple Online and Realtime Tracking"

content.title: General Feedback by Authors
content.comment:
We thank all the comments and suggestions from the reviewers. Here, we provide our feedback for some shared questions and make general clarification about this work here. 

1. **Motivation of OC-SORT:** With the rise of deep learning, the current dominant genre of multi-object tracking algorithms heavily, if not purely, rely on appearance matching while leaving the motion information unexplored. We were motivated by the observations that appearance matching can fail in many cases, such as presented in the DanceTrack dataset, to look deeply into the existing motion modeling. Then, we discover some intrinsic and long-standing flaws of the existing Kalman filter-based tracking methods. We develop OC-SORT to make the tracking more robust especially under occlusion and non-linear motion while keeping the algorithms simple, real-time, and online. 

2. **Novelty of OC-SORT:** We believe that OC-SORT shows good novelty and contribution including:

   1. First, Kalman-filter-based solutions are the most commonly adopted motion-based video tracking methods these days because of the good approximation of linear assumption in the high-frame-rate video. Existing non-linear filters, such as Extended Kalman Filter, etc, require pre-defined assumptions of the non-linear motion, which is impossible in practice. OC-SORT is the first we know that provides an analysis of the flaws of linear assumption by Kalman filter in tracking and a corresponding fixing of them. 

   2. Second, a core of developing OC-SORT is to keep it online. This makes a huge difference with some similar but fundamentally different solutions of off-line fitting, such as fix-lag smoother and fix-interval smoother, which typically can't be used in real-world tracking problems. Moreover, the performance gain of OC-SORT is significant without losing good time efficiency.

   3. Third, the two key components of OC-SORT, i.e. OOS and OCM, are proposed with theoretical analysis first. We were surprised that some flaws by the theoretical outcomes were obvious and the community have been suffering from them for a long time. We believe the theoretical discussion behind OC-SORT would be helpful for further solutions regarding the problem of failure of motion pattern assumption in motion-based tracking algorithms.

    Our experiments have demonstrated its effectiveness, especially in the case of heavy occlusion and non-linear motion on DanceTrack. OC-SORT achieves superior performance on multiple tracking datasets and its time efficiency can be 10 times or even faster than some other methods with comparable performance. 

3. **Why we think OC-SORT can be helpful to the community:**
 
   1. First of all, OC-SORT is helpful to the community because it has SoTA performance and superior time efficiency (700+FPS on a single CPU given detections). 

   2. Also, we have provided the source code of OC-SORT in the supplementary and make it public to the community here. The implementation is flexible to work with different detectors. For example, we use the YOLOX detector on MOT17/MOT20, PermaTrack detector on KITTI, FairMOT/HeadTrack detections on CroHD, etc.

   3. Finally, the implementations we provide are a clean and generalizable version that all hyper-parameters are shared on all datasets. It guarantees that the performance advantage does not come from careful parameter tuning but from the intrinsic improvement of the algorithm design. Moreover, further adopting some data-relevant heuristic techniques can further boost performance. For example, adopting the customized detection threshold used by ByteTrack on MOT17/MOT20 can make OC-SORT show higher MOTA/HOTA on these datasets. Also, using C-IoU or center distance instead of the naive IoU on KITTI can make OC-SORT achieve a higher HOTA score even on the fast-moving Car instances. 

   To summarize, in this work, we provide both theoretical analysis and experimental demonstrations of a solution to relieve the effect of non-linear motion and occlusion in motion-based tracking. We provide an effective, efficient but also clean, and generalizable source code for the use of the community. We believe OC-SORT can help follow-up works in this area.

4. **writing issues:** We have updated the paper draft where the edited content is highlighted in blue. We will keep polishing the writing of this paper to make it more readable and better organized. Moreover, because of the page limit, we had to move many key sections to the appendix. We would adjust the structure of this paper to make sure the key information can be in time provided in the proper positions.
